title: Limitations on Joint Coherence Transfer in Quantum Thermodynamics
abstract: Coherences between different energy levels are strongly constrained by thermodynamics. Here we ask a related question: if several coherence transfers can be optimized separately, can they also be optimized simultaneously by the same thermodynamic process? We show that this is in general a compatibility problem. Using an energy-resolved Stinespring representation of thermal operations, we express elementary coherence-transfer amplitudes as inner products of bath-weighted vectors associated with total-energy shells. Saturation of the corresponding Cauchy--Schwarz bounds requires these vectors to be collinear. Since all transfers have to arise from the same energy-preserving system--bath unitary, such saturation conditions cannot in general be imposed independently. Trace and Gibbs preservation lead to additional phase-closure conditions and to polygon inequalities that can rule out simultaneous saturation for fixed population-transfer data.   We complement these analytic results with a rigorous computer-assisted semidefinite-program analysis. For the mixed-degenerate Hamiltonian $H=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1,3)$, machine-certified primal and dual bounds show that no covariant Gibbs-preserving channel can simultaneously attain three individually optimal directional coherence transfers. Since every thermal operation is covariant and Gibbs preserving, the same triple of optimal values cannot be attained by a thermal operation. We further relate this incompatibility to range-inclusion constraints in Choi-sector Gram matrices for mixed-degenerate energy levels. Our results show that coherence transfers which are optimal when considered separately need not be compatible with one physical thermodynamic process. A full characterization of this incompatibility directly within thermal operations remains open.
summary: This paper investigates whether multiple individually optimal coherence transfers in a quantum system can be achieved simultaneously by one single thermodynamic process. Using advanced techniques including Stinespring representations and semidefinite programming, the authors prove that this joint optimization is generally impossible due to inherent compatibility constraints imposed by thermal operations. The results highlight a fundamental limitation on what physical processes can achieve when optimizing multiple distinct quantum coherence measures.
main_problem: The core problem is determining if multiple coherence transfers, each individually achievable optimally by a quantum process, can be simultaneously optimized by the same single thermodynamic process.
main_result: The authors prove that joint optimization of these coherence transfers is generally impossible for thermal operations, even when individual optimizations are possible. This incompatibility is rigorously demonstrated using semidefinite programming and algebraic constraints.
method: The analysis employs energy-resolved Stinespring representations, formulating the problem as a compatibility condition constrained by trace and Gibbs preservation laws, which leads to polygon inequalities and SDP formulations.
model_or_system: The study uses quantum thermodynamics applied to a system described by a mixed-degenerate Hamiltonian $H=	ext{diag}(0,1,1,3)$. The processes considered are thermal operations (TO), which must be covariant and Gibbs preserving.
key_observables: Coherence transfer amplitudes ($\Phi(|iangle\langle j|)$) and the feasibility of joint saturation for these transfers.
important_parameters: The structure of the mixed-degenerate Hamiltonian, population transfer data ($p_f$), and the constraints imposed by thermal operations (covariance, Gibbs preservation).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that any physical process must be a thermal operation derived from an energy-preserving system-bath unitary.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem by relating coherence transfers to inner products of bath-weighted vectors, establishing necessary conditions via Cauchy-Schwarz bounds. It then incorporates thermodynamic constraints (trace/Gibbs preservation) leading to inequalities and culminates in a rigorous SDP analysis proving incompatibility for specific cases.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental mathematical constraints on the operational capabilities of quantum systems under thermalization, showing that local optimization goals can conflict when constrained by global physical processes like energy conservation.
